fatal_errors: The proposed Q235 pre-oxidation treatment does not reconstruct the target intervention: an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L followed by a 2 h anneal, optimized at 550 °C.
It substitutes an Fe2O3/Fe3O4 scale mechanism for the target HEA-mediated mechanism involving coating microstructure, sluggish diffusion, and Al-/Cr-rich protective oxides.
The cited evidence concerns Al-rich oxides on HEA coatings and does not establish that air annealing bare Q235 at 700 °C creates a durable protective Fe-oxide scale in molten sulfate/chloride salts.
The room-temperature test uses unspecified mild saline rather than the target 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical regime, so it cannot address the intended cross-regime behavior.
Annealing and oxide formation are not independently controlled, leaving substrate microstructural changes confounded with the proposed scale effect.
explanation: The hypothesis is testable and includes a reasonable untreated baseline, microscopy, mass-change measurements, boundaries, and a falsification rule. It also overlaps superficially with the target hot-corrosion environment by using 75% Na2SO4/25% NaCl and 900 °C. Nevertheless, it describes a fundamentally different material, intervention, structural mediator, and protection mechanism. It omits the AlCoCrFeNi coating, APS parameters, 550 °C post-coating anneal, phase and grain-boundary changes, acid polarization and impedance measurements, cyclic exposure protocol, and vanadate-containing salts. The supporting papers show that Al-/Cr-containing HEA coatings can form protective oxide scales; they do not validate extrapolation to a thermally grown iron-oxide scale on bare Q235. Moreover, comparing annealed and untreated specimens cannot isolate oxide continuity from annealing-induced substrate changes. A stronger test would independently remove or reproduce the pre-oxide, include an inert-atmosphere annealed control, quantify scale adhesion and composition, and use matched cyclic mass-gain and electrochemical conditions.
